hypotheses.claim: ORM hydration of each Invoice (and its lazy-loaded FeeSchedule) consumes the bulk of per‑row latency
hypotheses.mechanism: Spring Data JPA loads an Invoice entity for each result row; the subsequent per‑row call to feeScheduleRepo.findByActiveTrue triggers a lazy load of the FeeSchedule entity, causing Hibernate to populate entity fields, proxies and collections for each row, which costs CPU and memory allocation.
evidence: p50 latency grows from 4.8 ms (1 row) to 58.9 ms (100 rows) ≈ 0.6 ms per row
server‑side SQL per request grows only from 0.3 ms to 4.5 ms (≈0.045 ms per row), so >90 % of the per‑row cost is not SQL
application SQL statements rise from 2 to 101, matching rows, yet SQL time remains tiny, implying the ORM still materialises entities for each row
hypotheses.prediction: If the repository method returns a projection DTO (bypassing entity hydration) the latency per row will drop by at least 50 % (e.g., 100‑row request latency <30 ms).

hypotheses.claim: JSON serialization of the result list dominates the remaining per‑row cost
hypotheses.mechanism: After ORM creates entity objects, Spring MVC (Jackson) walks each object's fields to write JSON; the work scales with number of objects and size of their fields, costing CPU proportional to body bytes.
evidence: response body size scales linearly: 119 bytes per row (1 row) vs 12 299 bytes for 100 rows
latency per row (≈0.6 ms) correlates with body bytes per row, while SQL time is negligible
Jackson's default serialization incurs reflection and object graph traversal for each entity
hypotheses.prediction: Switching to a streaming JSON writer or disabling pretty‑print will reduce latency per row by at least 20 % (e.g., 100‑row request latency drops by ~12 ms).

hypotheses.claim: Per‑row application logic (late‑fee calculation) adds measurable overhead beyond ORM and serialization
hypotheses.mechanism: For each invoice, the service fetches the active fee schedule (N+1) and computes a late‑fee amount; even though the DB fetch is cheap, the repeated query execution, result handling and arithmetic add CPU cycles per iteration.
evidence: OverdueWorklistService iterates each invoice row and invokes feeScheduleRepo.findByActiveTrue for each, incurring a method call and simple Java arithmetic per row
SQL time of that call is tiny (0.045 ms per row), so the Java call and fee calculation dominate that slice
Total per‑row latency (0.6 ms) exceeds the sum of ORM (≈0.4 ms from h1) and serialization (≈0.3 ms from h2), leaving a remainder consistent with extra Java work
hypotheses.prediction: Caching the active fee schedule (single query before the loop) will make latency independent of row count, reducing the 100‑row request latency by ~7 ms.

probes_run.result: Latency 4.8 ms for 1 row, SQL 0.3 ms, body 119 B. Shows per‑row cost ≈4.5 ms not explained by SQL.
Latency 58.9 ms for 100 rows, SQL 4.5 ms, body 12 299 B. Linear scaling of latency with rows while SQL stays small.
